report:
**Conclusion: no—overall, saw palmetto preparations have not been shown to improve BPH urinary symptoms more than placebo in the longer term.** Your sister’s answer is not supported by the strongest placebo-controlled evidence.

The most informative long-term randomized trial followed men for **72 weeks (18 months)** and tested escalating doses (up to three times the usual dose). Saw palmetto did not outperform placebo on the American Urological Association Symptom Index: the mean difference was **0.79 points in favor of placebo**, and even the confidence limit most favorable to saw palmetto was below a clinically important benefit. Thus, higher dosing did not rescue effectiveness.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439

Earlier high-quality evidence was consistent: an updated Cochrane systematic review reported that the one high-quality **12-month** placebo-controlled trial (225 participants) found no significant symptom difference. The review’s broader conclusion was that *Serenoa repens* (saw palmetto) monotherapy did not improve lower-urinary-tract symptoms versus placebo.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3513282/

This does not mean every product is chemically identical: extracts differ by preparation, and some European guidance discusses a specific **hexane extract**. But that is not evidence that ordinary over-the-counter “saw palmetto preparations” reliably provide meaningful long-term relief, and it should not be generalized across products.  
https://uroweb.org/guidelines/management-of-non-neurogenic-male-luts/chapter/disease-management

For someone with persistent urinary symptoms, evaluation matters because symptoms can have causes besides BPH and effective evidence-based treatments are available.
